claims.text: A controlled heat treatment that inverts the microstructure can concurrently improve strength and ductility in refractory high-entropy alloys.
The initial alloy has a continuous ordered B2 matrix with discrete or minor BCC precipitates.
The treatment includes solutionizing at 1400 °C for a short period followed by rapid quenching.
The treatment subsequently includes annealing at 600 °C for about 120 hours.
Mechanical performance is evaluated by room-temperature uniaxial compression at an initial strain rate of approximately 0.001 s⁻¹.
The heat treatment produces an inverted microstructure consisting of a continuous disordered BCC matrix and discrete ordered B2 precipitates.
The discrete B2 precipitates are approximately 50 nm in size.
A continuous disordered BCC matrix enhances ductility by providing a more malleable medium for dislocation motion.
Discrete B2 precipitates impede dislocation motion and provide precipitation strengthening.
The initial brittle state has a yield strength of approximately 2032 MPa and a compressive fracture strain of approximately 4.7%.
The inverted microstructure reaches approximately 38% fracture strain.
The inverted microstructure has a yield strength of approximately 1345 MPa.
The method maintains or moderately improves yield strength relative to the initial brittle state.
The method has been demonstrated under room-temperature compressive loading in a refractory high-entropy alloy.
Its effectiveness under tensile loading or in other alloy systems remains unverified.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says strength and ductility are concurrently improved, but the stated yield strength decreases from approximately 2032 MPa initially to approximately 1345 MPa after treatment.
The mechanism says yield strength is maintained or moderately improved, whereas the predicted values indicate a decrease of about 687 MPa relative to the initial state.
